title: Interconnects & Networks-on-Chip
summary: Why the on-chip communication fabric becomes the real scaling bottleneck as core counts grow, and the topologies that address it.

slides.markdown:
Cores are only as parallel as their ability to actually **communicate** — coherence traffic, shared-cache access, and memory requests all travel over some physical on-chip fabric connecting cores to each other and to memory. As core count grows, this fabric, not the cores themselves, increasingly determines whether adding more cores actually helps.

A chip with 64 fast cores and a weak interconnect can perform worse than one with 32 cores and a strong one, because contention on the fabric — not compute capacity — becomes the bottleneck.

A **shared bus** is the simplest interconnect: every core connects to one common set of wires, and only one core (or message) uses it at a time. It's cheap — and exactly why classic snooping coherence ([cache-coherence-protocols](cache-coherence-protocols)) relies on a bus, since every core can passively observe every transaction.

Its fatal flaw at scale: it's a **single point of contention** — total bandwidth is fixed regardless of core count, so more cores just means more contenders sharing one pipe. This is why bus-based designs top out at a handful of cores.

A **crossbar** gives every core a dedicated path to every other core/memory port simultaneously — any-to-any connectivity with no shared contention point, dramatically better bandwidth than a bus.

The cost is **quadratic**: connecting N cores to N ports needs on the order of N² switching elements, so a crossbar's area and power explode well before core counts reach even the dozens, making it impractical at the core counts modern chips actually target.

A **mesh (Network-on-Chip, NoC)** arranges cores in a grid, each tile connected only to its immediate neighbors; a message between distant cores hops tile-to-tile through the grid via routers, rather than needing a direct wire to every destination.

This is the scalable choice: adding a core adds one more tile with local connections only, so the interconnect's cost grows roughly linearly with core count instead of quadratically — the reason virtually every many-core chip (16+ cores) uses a mesh-style NoC rather than a bus or crossbar.

![Bus, crossbar, and mesh topologies compared for connecting 8 cores](assets/interconnect-topologies.svg)

The bus's single shared line bottlenecks first; the crossbar's every-to-every wiring is fast but explodes in complexity; the mesh's local links plus routed hops is what actually scales — why large core counts force a move toward NoC.

slides.markdown:
A NoC's cost isn't one number — it's the interaction of **latency** (time for one message to cross the fabric) and **bandwidth** (total data the fabric moves per second), and mesh topologies trade one against the other in a specific, countable way. In an NxN mesh, two cores on opposite corners are `2(N-1)` hops apart — an 8x8 mesh has a worst-case 14-hop path, and each hop adds a router traversal (typically 1-4 cycles) on top of wire delay.

This is why a crossbar (1 hop, any core to any core) and a mesh (variable hops, scales in area) aren't just "two options" — they sit at opposite ends of a real trade-off: a crossbar's wiring and arbitration logic grows as **O(N^2)** with core count (every core needs a direct link to every other), which is exactly why it stops being buildable much past 8-16 cores, while a mesh's router count grows as **O(N)**, at the cost of the multi-hop latency shown above.

Real high-core-count chips (64+ cores) universally choose mesh or similar scalable topologies for this reason — not because hop latency is free, but because O(N^2) wiring simply doesn't fit on a die at that core count.

A mesh needs a **routing algorithm** deciding which path a message takes between two non-adjacent routers, and the naive choice can deadlock the entire fabric. Consider four packets, each waiting for a buffer held by the next one in a cycle — A waits for B's buffer, B waits for C's, C waits for D's, D waits for A's — none can proceed, and the network is permanently stuck, not just slow.

The standard fix is **dimension-order routing (DOR)**: always route fully along the X dimension first, then fully along Y — e.g., XY routing. This provably cannot deadlock, because it establishes a strict partial order on buffer acquisition (no packet ever asks for a Y-direction buffer, then waits on an X-direction one that would complete a cycle) — a restriction that costs some path flexibility (it's not always the shortest possible route) in exchange for a hard correctness guarantee.

This deadlock-freedom analysis is a genuinely distinct concern from the raw latency/hop-count trade-off on the previous slide — a topology can have great average latency and still deadlock under adversarial traffic patterns if its routing algorithm doesn't rule it out structurally.

The interconnect isn't just carrying ordinary loads and stores — it's also the fabric that **cache-coherence traffic** rides on (invalidations, snoop requests, data forwarding between caches), and at high core counts this traffic can dominate total interconnect load, not the application's actual memory accesses.

A broadcast-based snooping protocol (viable on a shared bus with few cores) sends every cache miss to *every other core's* cache controller — traffic that grows roughly linearly with core count per miss, and multiplicatively with total miss rate. At 8 cores this is cheap; at 64+ cores, broadcasting every coherence event to every core would saturate a mesh fast. This is exactly why large core-count chips pair their NoC with a **directory-based** coherence protocol instead of snooping — a directory tracks which specific cores hold a given line, so an invalidation is unicast/multicast only to the actual sharers, not broadcast to all N cores.

The practical takeaway: interconnect topology and coherence protocol choice aren't independent decisions — a mesh's point-to-point nature is precisely what makes directory-based (point-to-point) coherence feasible at scale, where a shared bus's broadcast nature paired naturally with snooping instead.

It's worth anchoring interconnect cost against the alternative it's replacing. An on-chip mesh hop typically costs **1-4 cycles** of router latency plus wire propagation — a cross-chip message on a large mesh might total **10-30 cycles** end to end. Compare that to reaching off-chip DRAM, which costs **100-300+ cycles** round trip even on a fast memory controller, or reaching a remote NUMA node's memory over an inter-socket link (see memory-consistency-models' "why hardware relaxes it" context), which adds another 50-150+ cycles on top of local DRAM latency.

This ordering — on-chip mesh hop << local DRAM << remote NUMA access — is why software that understands the memory hierarchy actively pins threads and data to cores that are interconnect-close to each other (NUMA-aware allocation, core affinity) rather than treating "which core runs this thread" as a detail the scheduler can ignore. A thread migrated to a core far from its data on the mesh, or on a different NUMA socket entirely, pays real, measurable extra latency on every access that misses the local cache.
